Question 2: A Comparative Study of Clustering Algorithms

This question asks you to compare K-Means, Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering, and DBSCAN on two synthetic 2D datasets: Blobs and Moons

Part A: Finding the right “K” using K-Means on Blobs

1. Import libraries and generate the datasets

Python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs, make_moons
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, AgglomerativeClustering, DBSCAN
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

Explanation

This block imports everything we need:

  • numpy for numerical work

  • matplotlib.pyplot for plotting

  • make_blobs and make_moons to create the datasets required in the assignment

  • KMeans, AgglomerativeClustering, and DBSCAN for clustering

Now create the two datasets exactly as requested.

Python
# Dataset 1: Blobs
X_blobs, y_blobs = make_blobs(
    n_samples=300,
    centers=4,
    cluster_std=0.60,
    random_state=0
)

# Dataset 2: Moons
X_moons, y_moons = make_moons(
    n_samples=300,
    noise=0.05,
    random_state=0
)

Explanation

  • X_blobs contains the 2D points for the blob dataset.

  • X_moons contains the 2D points for the moon-shaped dataset.

  • The y_blobs and y_moons values are the true labels generated by sklearn, but clustering is unsupervised, so we do not use them for training. They are only useful for understanding the dataset.

2. Visualize the datasets first

Python
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))

plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.scatter(X_blobs[:, 0], X_blobs[:, 1], s=40, edgecolor='k')
plt.title("Dataset 1: Blobs")

plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
plt.scatter(X_moons[:, 0], X_moons[:, 1], s=40, edgecolor='k')
plt.title("Dataset 2: Moons")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Explanation

This gives you a quick visual understanding:

  • Blobs looks like several roughly circular groups.

  • Moons looks like two curved half-moon shapes.

This matters because some clustering algorithms work well for compact round clusters, while others can handle irregular shapes better.

3. Use the Elbow Method on the Blobs dataset

Python
inertias = []
k_values = range(1, 11)

for k in k_values:
    kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=0, n_init=10)
    kmeans.fit(X_blobs)
    inertias.append(kmeans.inertia_)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(k_values, inertias, marker='o')
plt.xlabel("Number of clusters (k)")
plt.ylabel("Inertia / WCSS")
plt.title("Elbow Method for K-Means on Blobs")
plt.xticks(k_values)
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

Explanation

The Elbow Method helps us choose a good number of clusters.

  • inertia_ is the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS).

  • Lower inertia means points are closer to their assigned cluster centers.

  • As k increases, inertia always decreases, but after a certain point the improvement becomes small.

  • The “elbow” is where the curve bends noticeably.

For this dataset, you should see the elbow around k = 4, which matches the dataset generation (centers=4).

4. Train K-Means using the chosen optimal K

Python
optimal_k = 4

kmeans_blobs = KMeans(n_clusters=optimal_k, random_state=0, n_init=10)
blob_labels = kmeans_blobs.fit_predict(X_blobs)
centroids = kmeans_blobs.cluster_centers_

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.scatter(X_blobs[:, 0], X_blobs[:, 1], c=blob_labels, s=40, cmap='viridis', edgecolor='k')
plt.scatter(centroids[:, 0], centroids[:, 1], c='red', s=250, marker='X', label='Centroids')
plt.title("K-Means Clustering on Blobs (k=4)")
plt.xlabel("Feature 1")
plt.ylabel("Feature 2")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Explanation

This block trains the final K-Means model on the blobs dataset.

  • fit_predict() both trains the model and returns the cluster labels.

  • cluster_centers_ gives the centroids of the clusters.

  • In the scatter plot:

    • each color represents a cluster

    • the red X markers represent the cluster centroids

What to write in your explanation

You can say:

Using the Elbow Method, the optimal number of clusters was found to be 4 because the inertia decreased sharply up to k=4 and then started decreasing more gradually. After fitting K-Means with k=4, the algorithm grouped the blob dataset successfully, and the centroids were located near the center of each blob. This is expected because K-Means performs well when clusters are compact, well-separated, and roughly spherical.

Part B: When Centroids Fail on the Moons Dataset

The assignment asks to apply both K-Means (with k=2) and Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering (n_clusters=2, linkage='ward') to the moons dataset

5. Apply K-Means to the Moons dataset

Python
kmeans_moons = KMeans(n_clusters=2, random_state=0, n_init=10)
moon_kmeans_labels = kmeans_moons.fit_predict(X_moons)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.scatter(X_moons[:, 0], X_moons[:, 1], c=moon_kmeans_labels, s=40, cmap='viridis', edgecolor='k')
plt.scatter(kmeans_moons.cluster_centers_[:, 0], kmeans_moons.cluster_centers_[:, 1],
            c='red', s=250, marker='X', label='Centroids')
plt.title("K-Means on Moons (k=2)")
plt.xlabel("Feature 1")
plt.ylabel("Feature 2")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Explanation

Here K-Means is forced to create exactly 2 clusters.

But the moons dataset is not made of two round blobs. Instead, it has two curved, interlocking shapes. K-Means tries to partition space based on distance to centroids, so it usually draws a roughly linear boundary and fails to recover the two moon shapes properly.

6. Apply Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering to the Moons dataset

Python
agglo = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=2, linkage='ward')
moon_agglo_labels = agglo.fit_predict(X_moons)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.scatter(X_moons[:, 0], X_moons[:, 1], c=moon_agglo_labels, s=40, cmap='viridis', edgecolor='k')
plt.title("Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering on Moons (n_clusters=2, linkage='ward')")
plt.xlabel("Feature 1")
plt.ylabel("Feature 2")
plt.show()

Explanation

Agglomerative clustering starts with each point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges clusters.

With linkage='ward', the algorithm merges clusters in a way that minimizes the increase in within-cluster variance. This often works somewhat like centroid-based compact clustering, so it also prefers clusters that are more compact and globular.

What to write in your explanation

You can say:

K-Means did not successfully separate the two moon-shaped clusters. Instead, it divided the dataset into two regions based on centroid distance, which is not suitable for curved shapes. Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering with Ward linkage also struggled because Ward linkage favors compact clusters and minimizes within-cluster variance. Since the moon shapes are non-convex and curved, both algorithms fail to capture the true geometry of the data.

A bit more detail:

  • Why K-Means fails

    • It assumes clusters are centered around means.

    • It works best when clusters are spherical or convex.

    • The moons are non-convex, so centroid-based splitting is a bad match.

  • Why Agglomerative with Ward fails

    • Ward linkage tries to keep variance low inside clusters.

    • This pushes it toward compact groups.

    • The moons are stretched and curved, not compact blobs.

Part C: DBSCAN to the Rescue

Now we use DBSCAN, which is a density-based clustering algorithm.

DBSCAN is often much better for data like moons because it groups points that are connected through dense neighborhoods rather than trying to place centroids.

7. Experiment with DBSCAN parameters

You were asked to tune eps and min_samples until the two moon shapes are separated properly

A very common good choice for this moons dataset is:

  • eps = 0.2

  • min_samples = 5

Try this first.

Python
dbscan = DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=5)
moon_dbscan_labels = dbscan.fit_predict(X_moons)

print("Unique cluster labels:", np.unique(moon_dbscan_labels))

Explanation

  • eps is the neighborhood radius.

  • min_samples is the minimum number of nearby points needed for a point to be considered a core point.

  • fit_predict() returns cluster labels.

  • If DBSCAN marks some points as noise, they get label -1.

For this dataset, eps=0.2 and min_samples=5 usually work very well.

8. Plot final DBSCAN result

Python
unique_labels = np.unique(moon_dbscan_labels)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))

for label in unique_labels:
    if label == -1:
        plt.scatter(
            X_moons[moon_dbscan_labels == label, 0],
            X_moons[moon_dbscan_labels == label, 1],
            s=40,
            c='black',
            marker='x',
            label='Noise'
        )
    else:
        plt.scatter(
            X_moons[moon_dbscan_labels == label, 0],
            X_moons[moon_dbscan_labels == label, 1],
            s=40,
            label=f'Cluster {label}'
        )

plt.title("DBSCAN on Moons")
plt.xlabel("Feature 1")
plt.ylabel("Feature 2")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Explanation

This plot shows the final clusters found by DBSCAN.

  • Each moon should appear as a separate cluster.

  • If there are any noise points, they will be shown with black x markers.

  • In a good parameter setting, DBSCAN can separate the two moon shapes almost perfectly.

Full code in one place

If you want one clean script to run directly, here it is:

Python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs, make_moons
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, AgglomerativeClustering, DBSCAN

# -----------------------------
# Generate datasets
# -----------------------------
X_blobs, y_blobs = make_blobs(
    n_samples=300,
    centers=4,
    cluster_std=0.60,
    random_state=0
)

X_moons, y_moons = make_moons(
    n_samples=300,
    noise=0.05,
    random_state=0
)

# -----------------------------
# Visualize datasets
# -----------------------------
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))

plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.scatter(X_blobs[:, 0], X_blobs[:, 1], s=40, edgecolor='k')
plt.title("Dataset 1: Blobs")

plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
plt.scatter(X_moons[:, 0], X_moons[:, 1], s=40, edgecolor='k')
plt.title("Dataset 2: Moons")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# -----------------------------
# Part A: Elbow Method for Blobs
# -----------------------------
inertias = []
k_values = range(1, 11)

for k in k_values:
    kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=0, n_init=10)
    kmeans.fit(X_blobs)
    inertias.append(kmeans.inertia_)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(k_values, inertias, marker='o')
plt.xlabel("Number of clusters (k)")
plt.ylabel("Inertia / WCSS")
plt.title("Elbow Method for K-Means on Blobs")
plt.xticks(k_values)
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

optimal_k = 4
kmeans_blobs = KMeans(n_clusters=optimal_k, random_state=0, n_init=10)
blob_labels = kmeans_blobs.fit_predict(X_blobs)
centroids = kmeans_blobs.cluster_centers_

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.scatter(X_blobs[:, 0], X_blobs[:, 1], c=blob_labels, s=40, cmap='viridis', edgecolor='k')
plt.scatter(centroids[:, 0], centroids[:, 1], c='red', s=250, marker='X', label='Centroids')
plt.title("K-Means Clustering on Blobs (k=4)")
plt.xlabel("Feature 1")
plt.ylabel("Feature 2")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

# -----------------------------
# Part B: K-Means on Moons
# -----------------------------
kmeans_moons = KMeans(n_clusters=2, random_state=0, n_init=10)
moon_kmeans_labels = kmeans_moons.fit_predict(X_moons)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.scatter(X_moons[:, 0], X_moons[:, 1], c=moon_kmeans_labels, s=40, cmap='viridis', edgecolor='k')
plt.scatter(kmeans_moons.cluster_centers_[:, 0], kmeans_moons.cluster_centers_[:, 1],
            c='red', s=250, marker='X', label='Centroids')
plt.title("K-Means on Moons (k=2)")
plt.xlabel("Feature 1")
plt.ylabel("Feature 2")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

# -----------------------------
# Part B: Agglomerative on Moons
# -----------------------------
agglo = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=2, linkage='ward')
moon_agglo_labels = agglo.fit_predict(X_moons)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.scatter(X_moons[:, 0], X_moons[:, 1], c=moon_agglo_labels, s=40, cmap='viridis', edgecolor='k')
plt.title("Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering on Moons")
plt.xlabel("Feature 1")
plt.ylabel("Feature 2")
plt.show()

# -----------------------------
# Part C: DBSCAN on Moons
# -----------------------------
dbscan = DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=5)
moon_dbscan_labels = dbscan.fit_predict(X_moons)

for label in unique_labels:

plt.title("DBSCAN on Moons")
plt.xlabel("Feature 1")
plt.ylabel("Feature 2")
plt.legend()

Written explanation for submission

You can use the following write-up in your PDF.

Part A: Finding the right K

For Dataset 1 (Blobs), I applied K-Means clustering and used the Elbow Method by plotting inertia against the number of clusters from 1 to 10. The curve showed a clear bend at k = 4, indicating that 4 is the optimal number of clusters. This matches the structure of the generated dataset, since the data was created with 4 centers. After fitting K-Means with k=4, the algorithm successfully grouped the data into four distinct clusters, and the centroids were located near the center of each blob.

Part B: When Centroids Fail

For Dataset 2 (Moons), I first applied K-Means with k=2. The algorithm did not separate the two moon-shaped groups correctly because K-Means relies on centroids and Euclidean distance, which works best for compact, spherical clusters. The moons dataset contains curved, non-convex shapes, so the resulting partition did not match the actual structure of the data.

I then applied Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering with n_clusters=2 and linkage='ward'. This method also struggled to recover the two moon shapes correctly. Ward linkage merges clusters in a way that minimizes within-cluster variance, which again favors compact clusters rather than curved structures. Therefore, it also fails to model the true geometry of the moons dataset.

Part C: Density-Based Clustering to the Rescue

Finally, I applied DBSCAN to the moons dataset and tuned the hyperparameters. A good setting was eps = 0.2 and min_samples = 5. With these values, DBSCAN was able to separate the two moon shapes very well.

DBSCAN succeeds because it is a density-based clustering algorithm. Instead of assuming clusters are centered around centroids or must be compact, it groups together points that are connected through dense neighborhoods. This allows DBSCAN to detect clusters with arbitrary shapes, including the curved moon structures. That is why it performs much better than K-Means and Agglomerative Clustering on this dataset.

Important note for your output

When you run the code, your exact plots may look slightly different in color arrangement, but the clustering behavior should be the same.

Also, for DBSCAN, if eps=0.2 does not perfectly separate the moons on your machine, try small nearby values such as:

Python
DBSCAN(eps=0.18, min_samples=5)
DBSCAN(eps=0.22, min_samples=5)
DBSCAN(eps=0.20, min_samples=4)

because DBSCAN is sensitive to parameter tuning.
